reading.body:
Health insurance is where AI makes coverage decisions at scale, and where the rules governing those decisions are being written fastest.

The ten parts split into three layers. Algorithms decide: prior authorization scores a request against coverage criteria before payment, claims adjudication flags post-service claims in batches, and fraud detection models scan providers and billing patterns. Rules constrain: CMS limits on prior authorization, state utilization review laws that name who may decide medical necessity, and HIPAA following data into vendor systems. Liability follows: the Medicare Advantage denial lawsuits over nH Predict and similar tools, insurer exposure to bad faith and breach of contract claims, and providers building their own automation to answer algorithmic denials.

For AI specifically, this is the clearest case where the model's output is a payment or a denial rather than a recommendation. That makes the feedback loop tight. A denial is a data point, an appeal is a data point, and a lawsuit is a data point, all attached to a specific decision. It also means the governance is not voluntary. The CMS rules, the state laws, and the litigation are external constraints on how the model may be built and who may sign off on its output.

What the data does not cover is scale. There are no counts of denials, no error rates, no adoption figures, and no dollar amounts. It names the mechanisms and the legal instruments, not their size. It also does not say how any of the lawsuits resolved, or whether the state laws have been tested in court.

The three layers are not sequential stages of a pipeline. They are three clocks running at different speeds on the same decision. The algorithm layer changes whenever a model is retrained or a threshold is moved. The rules layer changes when CMS issues guidance or a state legislature passes a utilization review statute. The liability layer changes when a court rules or a case settles. A single denial can be produced by a model that was updated last month, judged under a rule written last year, and litigated under a theory that will not resolve for years. The insurer has to build for all three at once, which is why the governance burden here is heavier than in domains where only one clock runs.

The comparison the data supports is between the two federal programs and everything else. Medicare Advantage and the marketplace are the only settings where the page identifies federal rules on AI coverage decisions as developed enough to have their own treatment. Commercial plans appear in the prior authorization description alongside them, but the rules that limit the algorithms are described as federal and program-specific. State utilization review laws fill the gap for everything the federal programs do not reach, and California's Physicians Make Decisions Act is the named example. The practical consequence is that a plan operating across Medicare Advantage, the marketplace, and commercial lines faces three different constraint sets on the same underlying model.

The tightest loop in the data is the one between the denial and the lawsuit. The Medicare Advantage denial lawsuits are described as class actions over nH Predict and similar tools used to cut off post-acute and rehabilitation care. That is a specific clinical category, not denials in general. The liability page then lists the theories that follow: bad faith, breach of contract, unfair business practice, and the errors and omissions and D&O exposure behind them. So the litigation risk is concentrated where a model's output ends a course of care rather than where it prices a premium or flags a claim for review.

What is prior authorization AI and how does it differ from claims adjudication AI?
Prior authorization software scores a request against coverage criteria before a plan will pay. Claims adjudication runs after the service, where a system flags claims as not matching a diagnosis or coverage rule and a reviewer signs off on many at once. The first gates care before it happens, the second reviews payment after it has.

Which insurers are named in the Medicare Advantage denial lawsuits?
UnitedHealth, Cigna and Humana are named in the blurb. The lawsuits are class actions over nH Predict and similar tools used to cut off post-acute and rehabilitation care for Medicare Advantage members.

What does California's Physicians Make Decisions Act do?
The data names it as a state utilization review law, in a category described as laws that say who may make a medical necessity decision. The new ones in that category are written specifically about algorithms. The data does not include the text of the statute or its effective date.

Can an insurer use AI to decide whether to accept a risk or what to charge?
The underwriting and pricing page covers what an insurer may use to price or accept a risk when the model can infer far more than the application asks. The data does not state which inputs are permitted or prohibited.

Does HIPAA apply to an insurer's AI vendor?
The privacy page covers what an insurer's model may learn from and the HIPAA rules that follow the data into the vendor's system. The data does not specify which vendor arrangements trigger which obligations.

How did the Medicare Advantage denial lawsuits resolve?
The data does not say. It also does not say whether the state utilization review laws have been tested in court. There are no counts of denials, no error rates, no adoption figures, and no dollar amounts anywhere in it.
